title: How Nongfu Spring Made the Water Bottle That Swept the Design Awards
excerpt: Several design teams, Horse among them, submitted 58 rounds and more than 300 proposals before the Chinese beverage company was finally satisfied.
body:
Several design teams, Horse among them, submitted 58 rounds and more than 300 proposals before the Chinese beverage company was finally satisfied.

"We loved the design on paper, but it was just so hard to make. For all sorts of reasons, we came to fear it might never be made at all." Looking back on the packaging her team designed for Nongfu Spring, the British designer Sarah Pidgeon still marvels at how long and tangled the process was. From taking on the project to producing a sample bottle took about two and a half years, which is rare in packaging design.

Pidgeon is a partner at Horse, a British design studio. Before the studio existed, she had worked on Nongfu Spring packaging several times. But the job that really made the studio's name was the latest one: the packaging for Nongfu Spring's water in glass bottles.

Nongfu Spring launched the glass-bottled water in early 2015. The teardrop-shaped bottle shows plants and animals typical of the Changbai Mountains, where the water comes from, along with figures and short captions. Each number means something.

Two years in the making, the design swept almost every major packaging award of 2015: the FAB Awards (the international Food and Beverage Creative Excellence Awards), the UK's D&AD (Design and Art Direction) awards, the international Pentawards for packaging design, and the annual awards of the packaging-design publication The Dieline.

[The UK's Design Week Awards also gave it their only packaging prize of 2015](https://www.designweek.co.uk/design-week-awards-2015-the-winners/), calling it "elegant and beautiful," "a collector's item, very simple, and the delicate printing makes it look almost three-dimensional."

Meanwhile the water began turning up in high-end restaurants and at forums and conferences, and went on sale online. A 750ml bottle costs 45 yuan, more than any other Chinese-made bottled water.

For now, a mineral water this finely packaged and this expensive is an oddity among Chinese bottled waters. How did its design come about? We went looking for the story.

![Nongfu Spring glass-bottled water](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122631XQupvmJKyLbSWT0l.jpg-w600)

![Nongfu Spring glass-bottled water](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122631FcxtNoHOQh3q5bKC.jpg-w600)

By the time Nongfu Spring first approached Horse, the project was already a year old. Another studio was working on designs for the product, but Nongfu Spring wanted fresher ideas, so it brought in Horse.

The brief was clear. "They wanted a beautiful bottle, completely unique, that could express the stunning landscape of the source," Pidgeon recalls. "It had to be a bespoke shape, and to reflect the purity of the water it had to be clear and transparent." According to Zhou Zhenhua, assistant to Nongfu Spring's general manager, the bottle had to tell consumers at a glance that it held water, not liquor; it also had to reflect the local culture of the Changbai Mountains and draw consumers' attention to it.

Pidgeon and her team did a lot of work to understand the brief. Developing the concept alone took a long time. They began by listing the questions the design had to answer, then worked through them one by one, helped by market research, visits to the company, and study of Nongfu Spring's past products and the design material it had built up over the years.

Nongfu Spring said it wanted the mountains' plants and animals on the bottle, and simply invited the designers to the Changbai Mountains to see the setting of the source, Moya Spring, for themselves. "I can't imagine we would have grasped how amazing it is there if we hadn't gone. The place is full of inspiration. It fired us up, and by the time we got back to the studio we were completely motivated." The source lies inside a nature reserve, and the designers studied the plants and animals that live there.

We can't know whether Pidgeon had the moment that makes you leap out of your chair shouting "Eureka!" But she did read material Nongfu Spring gave her, mostly data and facts about the source, and these are said to have given her the idea.

"I remember one fact said the area is covered in snow 270 days a year. We realized at once that the design should try to express all these interesting facts," Pidgeon told QDaily.

So the final bottles carry eight species of plants and animals typical of the Changbai Mountains, and whether a bottle shows an animal or a plant tells you whether the water is sparkling. The illustrations are by the British illustrator Natasha Searston. She drew a Siberian tiger padding slowly forward, an antlered red deer, an osprey in flight and an alert scaly-sided merganser; the still water bottles show Komarov crabapple, Korean pine, wild ferns and snowflakes.

The drawings are very detailed, so to keep them from looking busy the bottles use only two color pairs, red and white or red and green. Apart from the large brand name, red picks out a single number on each bottle. That number is one of the "interesting facts" Pidgeon mentioned: the Changbai Mountain Nature Reserve has 48 known species of wild mammals and 94 known families of wild flowering plants; fewer than 1,000 scaly-sided mergansers, a species that has survived since the Tertiary ice age, remain in the world.

![Nongfu Spring glass-bottled water](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031226312cIoDuaLhpSm146N.jpg-w600)

![Nongfu Spring glass-bottled water](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122632b8Qvmr1d0GA9XKqp.jpg-w600)

The road from first sketches to final design was far from smooth. At one point the project stalled for a whole year, and Pidgeon began to doubt it would ever be finished. Nongfu Spring had approved Horse's design by June 2012, but bottle-making and printing techniques could not fully reproduce it: the bottle is curved, while the illustrations are fine and cover a large area, which demands top-grade machines and skill. Nongfu Spring could not say clearly how to fix it, so the project was put on hold. For a while the company looked elsewhere for other designs.

As the project dragged on, the design bill grew, both for hiring designers and for round after round of revisions. Over the whole development period, the international studios invited to pitch [included, besides Horse, Pearlfisher from the UK, Rossetti Design from Italy and StudioIn from Russia](http://www.dinghu.com/article/content/201511/59/1.html). Because of cultural gaps between the foreign designers and the company, and different ideas of what bottled water should be, Nongfu Spring was never quite happy with the details.

Some bottles looked more like liquor bottles or trophies than water. Some caps were too big and awkward to grip when opening. Others said something about water that was too generic and failed to capture what sets the Changbai Mountains apart. It even came down to the animals' expressions: a tiger that looked unfriendly or aloof could be reason enough to reject a design.

"Look at this tiger's eyes. They went through many revisions until the tiger felt natural. We didn't want a cartoon tiger, and we didn't want a ferocious one. It had to strike a balance. Then there's whether to draw it in profile or head-on, plus the limited space on the label... A lot goes into it," Zhou told QDaily.

After nearly two years of comparing options, Nongfu Spring decided in 2014 that dropping Horse's design would be a waste. It went back to the designers, and together they worked out how to reshape the bottle, fix the details and improve the production process. By the time the design was signed off, the design teams, Horse included, had submitted 58 rounds and more than 300 proposals, and only then did the Chinese beverage company make up its mind.

![Meant to be drunk with meals, the water could not come in packaging that looked too much like liquor](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122633du9eDHTUZqbyKL3S.jpg-w600)

If you follow packaging design, you may know that Nongfu Spring takes packaging more seriously than most of its Chinese rivals. Its Oriental Leaf tea drink and its Da Nai Cha milk tea both won silver in the beverage category at the Pentawards.

"Packaging is the most direct way to talk to consumers," Zhou says. "The product sits on the shelf where consumers can see it. Whatever message you want the product to send, packaging is the best carrier. So we think what we want to tell consumers should show in the design, so they know at first glance what we're trying to do."

That goes double for premium water.

Nongfu Spring took longer to launch this product than many expected. [In 2010 it overtook Wahaha, taking second place in China's bottled-water market with a 17.5% share](http://money.163.com/13/0618/14/91LISGQG002526O3.html), behind Master Kong, and it has stayed in the top two ever since. Yet before Nongfu Spring's glass bottle arrived, brands with smaller shares, such as 5100 Tibet Glacier Mineral Water, Evergrande Spring, Kunlun Mountain mineral water and Alkaqua, had already marketed their products as "premium water."

Against that background, Nongfu Spring's [general manager Zhong Shanshan explained the business case for the glass-bottled water in an interview with *Packaging & Design* magazine](http://www.dinghu.com/article/content/201511/59/1.html). First, it would fill a gap: high-end Chinese conferences and restaurants had no premium domestic water. Second, demand had been splitting into ever finer segments in recent years, premium water had become fashionable, and foreign brands were heating up competition at home, so a brand's product range had to divide accordingly. But finding a suitable source took nearly three years, and the packaging design hit its own snags, so the glass-bottled water did not reach the market until 2015.

Judging by its price and packaging, the product is not really aimed at Evergrande Spring or Kunlun Mountain, but at imported glass-bottled waters such as Perrier, San Pellegrino and VOSS, which have been showing up more and more at high-end restaurants and events in China. Just this January, [the Chinese company Reignwood Group bought a 50% stake in Norway's VOSS](http://finance.ifeng.com/a/20160112/14162321_0.shtml). Reignwood holds the exclusive rights to sell Red Bull in China and runs a huge distribution network, which VOSS hopes will help it grow in the Chinese market.

![Uni-President's Alkaqua is another Chinese mineral water with "ideas" in its packaging: you can read extra product information printed on the back of the label through the bottle, which works like a magnifying glass. Very refined.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122633f2N4biuarzFgelyv.jpg-w600)

![Perrier](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122633XdIF8t0T3hDuWeyl.gif-w600Gif)

![The Norwegian brand VOSS has won many fans with its striking packaging](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122634rTg3sX61U4jVRvkp.jpg-w600)

In early 2015, alongside the glass-bottled water, Nongfu Spring also launched a water for babies and toddlers and a natural mineral water for students, both with distinctive packaging. The baby water's bottle is shaped around the way a hand grips it; the student water carries cartoon illustrations by a foreign illustrator and a cap designed to resist spills.

Observers saw this as a brand upgrade for Nongfu Spring: three products for three carefully defined groups of consumers, with the move into premium water as its chance to break through its growth ceiling.

Zhou's response: "Everyone wants to make a good product. But what counts as good changes as a company grows, matures and broadens its horizons."

On packaging alone, the company's water used to mean the ordinary red-labeled bottle of mineral water, which needed only the most basic packaging and label. The glass bottle is far more complex and pulls in many more departments.

Nongfu Spring has an in-house department that coordinates packaging design. It draws the product's story out of the brand (the specific things it wants to tell consumers), uses that story to find the designers who best fit the product's character, and works with them. Once the designers have delivered their many ideas, the department brings in the industrial-design team to deal with printing and bottle-making, so that the design can actually be made and go smoothly into production.

The whole process later became material for advertising. At a product launch in February 2015, Nongfu Spring released a series of polished ad films showing its Changbai Mountain source and its factory, along with interviews in which the designers explained their ideas to consumers.

Zhou says the original aim was only to keep a record for the company's history. They took cameramen into the Changbai Mountains to film the building of the plant, the surveying of the source, the design process and more, and the people on screen were simply going about their work. Only after the footage piled up did the company decide to cut it into ads telling consumers how the product came to be.

![Nongfu Spring ad film footage](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122634FKfJYr02oWTP7aMl.jpg-w600)

![Nongfu Spring ad film footage](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703122635w6CUTj1v5yELk8dO.jpg-w600)

![Nongfu Spring's ads show how the product came to be, using footage from a documentary the company first shot for its own records](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031226356QXIShCunGw9e07W.jpg-w600)

It was a serious effort. Nongfu Spring has not released further sales figures, but judging by consumer comments scattered across social networks, many people remember details such as the water's source, and can tell from the packaging that the company is trying to do something different.

Image sources: Nongfu Spring, [Redhotmarketingblender](http://www.redhotmarketingblender.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/12/perrier-chit-chat-bottle.gif), [ALKAQUA](http://www.alkaqua.com.cn/wp-content/themes/alkaqua/product.php), [Springwater](http://www.springwater.nl/wp-content/images/vossrange1.jpg)
